blackman1998_origin.title: Technical note: IMS celebrates thirty years as an IBM product
blackman1998_origin.author: K. R. Blackman
blackman1998_origin.venue: IBM Systems Journal, Volume 37, Number 4, 1998, pp. 596-603
blackman1998_origin.quote: North American Rockwell won the bid to launch the first spacecraft to the moon, and in 1965 they established a partnership with IBM to fulfill the requirement for an automated system to manage large bills of material for the construction of the spacecraft.
supports: Rockwell won the bid to launch the first spacecraft to the moon
1965 partnership with IBM
the requirement was an automated system for large bills of material
blackman1998_origin.note: Quote is on p. 596. Naming caveat: Blackman, writing in 1998, uses the post-merger name "North American Rockwell" for 1965-66 events. The entity that won the bid and signed with IBM was North American Aviation; it became North American Rockwell only when it merged with Rockwell-Standard in September 1967. The prose follows the source's naming. By the story's dateline, 14 August 1968, the name is correct.

blackman1998_team.title: Technical note: IMS celebrates thirty years as an IBM product
blackman1998_team.author: K. R. Blackman
blackman1998_team.venue: IBM Systems Journal, Volume 37, Number 4, 1998, pp. 596-603
blackman1998_team.quote: In 1966, 12 members of the IBM team working with 10 members from North American Rockwell and 3 members from Caterpillar Tractor started the design and development of the Information Control System (ICS) and Data Language/I (DL/I).
supports: 1966 start of design and development
team of 12 IBM, 10 North American Rockwell, 3 Caterpillar Tractor
the two things built were ICS and DL/I
blackman1998_team.note: Quote is on p. 596. Same naming caveat as blackman1998_origin: in 1966 the 10-person partner team was North American Aviation's. Same page: "During the design and development process, the IBM team was moved to Los Angeles and increased to 21 members." Blackman gives no reason for Caterpillar Tractor's presence on the team.

blackman1998_ready.title: Technical note: IMS celebrates thirty years as an IBM product
blackman1998_ready.author: K. R. Blackman
blackman1998_ready.venue: IBM Systems Journal, Volume 37, Number 4, 1998, pp. 596-603
blackman1998_ready.quote: In April 1968, ICS was installed. The first “IMS READY” message was displayed on an IBM 2740 terminal at the Rockwell Space Division in Downey, California, on August 14, 1968. ICS was renamed Information Management System/360 in 1969.
supports: ICS installed April 1968
first “IMS READY” message on an IBM 2740 terminal
Rockwell Space Division, Downey, California
14 August 1968
renamed Information Management System/360 in 1969

blackman1998_hier.title: Technical note: IMS celebrates thirty years as an IBM product
blackman1998_hier.author: K. R. Blackman
blackman1998_hier.venue: IBM Systems Journal, Volume 37, Number 4, 1998, pp. 596-603
blackman1998_hier.quote: Because data are always accessed hierarchically, when a lock on a root segment is obtained, IMS determines whether any application programs hold locks on dependent segments.
supports: IMS data are always accessed hierarchically
root segment and dependent segments
blackman1998_hier.note: Quote is on p. 598, where it is the premise for an IMS locking optimisation; the proposition it states about IMS is carried independently on p. 596: "The IMS database management system (DBMS) implemented the hierarchical model tree structure to organize the collection of records in a one-to-many entity-relationship data model." and "Navigational access to the data for application code is through the DL/I standard callable interface data manipulation language (DML)."

blackman1998_today.title: Technical note: IMS celebrates thirty years as an IBM product
blackman1998_today.author: K. R. Blackman
blackman1998_today.venue: IBM Systems Journal, Volume 37, Number 4, 1998, pp. 596-603
blackman1998_today.quote: Today, over 90 percent of the top worldwide companies in the areas of manufacturing, finance, banking, retailing, aerospace, communications, government, insurance, high technology, and health care use IMS to run their daily operations.
supports: as of 1998, over 90 percent of the top worldwide companies in those sectors ran IMS daily
blackman1998_today.note: Quote is on p. 597 and carries footnote marker 1 in the printed original; cited reference 1 of the note reads "From SHARE Session 1226 presentation (February 26, 1998)." So the figure's stated provenance is an IBM user-group presentation, not an audit: a vendor-authored, dated 1998 number. The prose and the deck both attribute it to IBM rather than stating it flat. The paper's own summary, p. 603, gives a second form of the same claim: "Over 90 percent of the Fortune 1000 companies use IMS as their DBMS of choice."

codd1970.title: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks
codd1970.author: E. F. Codd
codd1970.venue: Communications of the ACM, Volume 13, Number 6, June 1970, pp. 377-387
codd1970.quote: 1.2.3. Access Path Dependence. Many of the existing formatted data systems provide users with tree-structured files or slightly more general network models of the data. Application programs developed to work with these systems tend to be logically impaired if the trees or networks are changed in structure.
supports: Codd names the defect “access path dependence”
section number is 1.2.3, not 1.1.3
byline reads IBM Research Laboratory, San Jose, California
journal header reads Volume 13 / Number 6 / June, 1970
codd1970.note: Section 1.2.3 heading and the tree/network sentences are on p. 378; 1.2.1 is Ordering Dependence and 1.2.2 is Indexing Dependence, so access path dependence is the third of three. Venue confirmed from the PDF's own running head, "Volume 13 / Number 6 / June, 1970 ... Communications of the ACM 377" through "387", and the byline "E. F. CODD, IBM Research Laboratory, San Jose, California".

codd1970_fail.title: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks
codd1970_fail.author: E. F. Codd
codd1970_fail.venue: Communications of the ACM, Volume 13, Number 6, June 1970, pp. 377-387
codd1970_fail.quote: If a program P is developed for this problem assuming one of the five structures above-that is, P makes no test to determine which structure is in effect-then P will fail on at least three of the remaining structures.
supports: Codd's worked example is parts and projects, drawn as five legal hierarchies
a program written for one hierarchy fails on at least three of the others
codd1970_fail.note: Quote is on p. 379 (Structures 1-5 are set up on p. 378). Hyphens shown are the printed en-dashes as OCR'd from the PDF. Scope caveat: Codd's five structures hold parts, projects and the quantity of a part committed to a project - a parts-to-projects commitment, not a parts-to-subassemblies bill of materials. Codd's bill of materials is a separate example on the same page, the ternary relation component, of which he writes: "It is a relation which plays a critical role in the parts explosion problem." Same p. 379: "Since, in general, it is not practical to develop application programs which test for all tree structurings permitted by the system, these programs fail when a change in structure becomes necessary."

unverified: The often-repeated 'two million parts' (or 'millions of parts') figure for the Saturn V / Apollo bill of materials. Blackman 1998 says only 'large bills of material'; no primary source for a part count was opened.

That the system was built for the Apollo programme and the Saturn V second stage by those names. Blackman 1998 says only 'the first spacecraft to the moon'; the Apollo/Saturn V naming appears in secondary sources (Wikipedia) that were not traceable to an opened primary.
Uri Berman as 'father of DL/I' and the $100,000 IBM Outstanding Contribution Award; Pete/Peter Nordyke of Rockwell. Both appear only in Wikipedia; the cited underlying sources were not reachable.

Vern Watts as IMS chief architect from 1966. An IBM Corporate staff article of February 2002 mirrored at vcwatts.org was opened but does not state the 1966 start, Berman, or the bill-of-materials part count.
Charles Bachman, 'The Programmer as Navigator' (CACM 16(11), November 1973) and the 1974 SIGFIDET Codd-Bachman debate. Every full-text host tried returned 403; not quoted, so not used in the prose.

Any currency figure for the cost of the programme, of the IMS development, or of a modern IMS core-system replacement. None could be verified, so O9's money clause is carried by the team headcount and the 1998 install-base figure instead.

Why Caterpillar Tractor supplied 3 of the 25 people on the ICS/DL/I team. Blackman 1998 records the headcount and nothing else; the obvious explanation (a tractor is a bill of materials too) is inference, not source, so it was removed from card p1c13-c2.

That Codd's five-structure worked example is itself a bill of materials. It is parts and projects with a committed quantity; his bill of materials is the separate component relation on the same page. Card p1c13-c1 was corrected to say "parts and projects" only.
